notes.meaning: Elisha warned the Shunammite woman whose son he had raised to life that a severe famine was coming on Israel for seven years. This famine was a judgment from the Lord because the people refused to repent of their idols. The woman trusted the prophet's word and moved her family to live among the Philistines until the hard years passed.

When the seven years ended, the woman returned home and found that others had taken over her family property while she was away. Because ancient widows were often helpless against land-grabbers, she went straight to the king's court to ask for justice. She wanted to make sure she was not ruined for having obeyed God's prophet.

King Jehoram of Israel happened to be talking with Gehazi, who had served Elisha. The king was eager to hear firsthand accounts of the miraculous things God had done through the prophet. God used the king's curiosity to set the stage to help the woman.

At the exact second Gehazi was describing how Elisha raised a dead child, the Shunammite woman and her son walked into the room to make her appeal. Gehazi immediately pointed them out to the king as living proof of the story. God orchestrated the timing so that her petition would receive the king's full attention and sympathy.

After the woman confirmed the story, the king appointed an official to see that all her property was given back. He also ordered that she receive all the income the fields had produced during the seven years she was away. In this way, God fully restored what she had lost while she was walking in obedience.

Elisha traveled to Damascus, the capital city of Aram, led by the Spirit of God. King Ben-hadad was lying sick in bed and was told that the famous prophet from Israel had arrived. Though the king had once tried to capture Elisha as an enemy, his sickness made him look to God's messenger for help.

Ben-hadad sent his chief officer, Hazael, to meet Elisha with a generous gift. He asked Hazael to inquire of the Lord whether he would recover from his sickness. Even though Ben-hadad worshiped pagan idols in his health, his suffering drove him to seek an answer from the true God.

Hazael arrived before Elisha with forty camel loads of the finest goods from Damascus to show deep respect. He delivered the king's message with humility, referring to Ben-hadad as Elisha's 'son.' The grand display was meant to win a favorable word from the prophet about the king's health.

Elisha gave an answer with two sides: Ben-hadad's sickness itself was not fatal, but the king was still going to die. God revealed to Elisha that a violent death was coming through the messenger standing before him. Hazael heard that the king could live, but Elisha knew Hazael would cut that life short.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note an ancient Hebrew copyist question here between the written text reading 'You will not live' and the traditional reading 'Tell him: You will surely live.' Modern translations generally follow the ancient versions and render it as a message to the king that he could recover from the disease itself.

notes.meaning: Elisha stared intently at Hazael until Hazael became deeply embarrassed and looked away. The prophet saw straight into Hazael's dark heart and understood the cruel plans forming there. The weight of that future evil caused the prophet to break down in tears.

When Hazael asked why he was weeping, Elisha described the brutal atrocities Hazael would inflict on Israel. Hazael would burn down their fortresses, slaughter their young men, crush their children, and murder expectant mothers. Elisha wept because he loved his people and grieved over the horrors of coming warfare.

Hazael protested by calling himself a 'mere dog,' meaning someone far too lowly and unimportant to accomplish such great deeds. Elisha answered plainly that the Lord had revealed Hazael would become the next king of Aram. Once he had royal power in his hands, his hidden cruelty would fully show itself.

Hazael returned to his master and chose to tell only half the truth. He told Ben-hadad that the prophet said he would recover, while hiding the warning that he was about to die. By lulling the king into a false sense of safety, Hazael made his treason much easier to carry out.

The very next day, Hazael soaked a thick bed coverlet in water and spread it over the sick king's face until he suffocated. The wet cloth left no outward marks of violence, making the murder look like a natural death. Ben-hadad died, and Hazael seized the throne just as God had foreseen.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient Assyrian records, such as an inscription from Shalmaneser, refer to Hazael as a commoner who seized the Syrian throne, confirming biblical records that he was a usurper without royal ancestry.

notes.meaning: Jehoram became king over Judah during the fifth year of King Joram of Israel, beginning his rule alongside his father Jehoshaphat before reigning on his own. He was thirty-two years old when he took the throne and ruled in Jerusalem for eight years. His brief reign proved to be disastrous for the spiritual life of Judah.

Jehoram abandoned the godly example of his father and copied the wicked ways of the kings of northern Israel. He had married Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, and her idolatry infected his heart and leadership. Entering into close ties with an ungodly family brought ruin to his kingdom.

Even though Jehoram deserved swift judgment, the Lord refused to wipe out the kingdom of Judah. God remained faithful to His promise to David that his family would always have a 'lamp,' meaning a royal descendant upon the throne. God preserved the line of David down through history until it culminated in Jesus Christ the Messiah.

During Jehoram's reign, the nation of Edom rebelled against Judah's rule and set up its own king. Edom had been subject to Judah since the days of King David roughly 150 years earlier. God used this loss of control as a chastisement to expose Jehoram's weakness and punish his sin.

Jehoram marched out to Zair with his war chariots to crush the rebellion, but the Edomites surrounded his camp. He launched a night attack to cut his way out, but his army broke rank and fled back to their homes. The military campaign failed completely to bring Edom back under Judah's authority.

Edom secured its independence from Judah from that time forward. At the same time, the priestly fortress city of Libnah within Judah also broke away in revolt. Jehoram's unfaithfulness to God caused his kingdom to fracture both along its borders and from within.

The other events of Jehoram's reign were recorded in the official royal chronicles of Judah. When he died, he was buried in the City of David, though not in the honored tombs of the kings, and his son Ahaziah took the throne. His ungodly life ended in dishonor and pain after a short reign.

Ahaziah took power in Judah during the twelfth year of King Joram of Israel. At this point in history, both the northern and southern kingdoms had kings with closely related names, reflecting the close ties between the two royal houses. This alliance brought northern idolatry straight into Jerusalem.

Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for only one year. His mother was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri and daughter of Ahab and Jezebel. Her corrupt family background heavily influenced Ahaziah during his brief time on the throne.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars widely recognize the reading of forty-two years in Second Chronicles 22:2 as an early scribal copying error, since Ahaziah's father died at age forty; the twenty-two years recorded here is accepted as the original number.

notes.meaning: Ahaziah followed the idolatrous practices of Ahab's family and did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord. Because his mother Athaliah was Ahab's daughter, Ahaziah listened to her ungodly counsel rather than God's law. Choosing ungodly companions and family ties led directly to his spiritual downfall.

Ahaziah joined his uncle, King Joram of Israel, in a military campaign against Hazael of Aram at Ramoth-gilead. During the battle, the Syrian archers wounded Joram, repeating the very disaster that had claimed Ahab's life years earlier. The military alliance tied Judah's fortunes directly to the corrupt house of Ahab.

King Joram withdrew to the royal city of Jezreel to recover from the battle wounds he received at Ramah. Ahaziah traveled down from Jerusalem to visit his sick uncle and ally. In God's providence, this visit placed Ahaziah in Jezreel at the very moment God's judgment was about to fall on Ahab's entire household.
